name: Uma Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, so you can separate what you'd say openly from what you think privately. What is a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior developer at a tech company that makes library lending software. I fix small bugs in overdue notices and book returns, then ask a senior colleague to check my changes. I earned a two-year college diploma after work in another field, so I'm still learning and slower than the experienced developers. I like it when a librarian says a child finally got the right notice instead of a wrong fine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What supports the household, and what worries you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs buses and we have two children, ten and fourteen, and a mortgage. My developer pay is typical for this work, and we've saved roughly four months of expenses. There are some software jobs nearby. I use AI now and then after someone else tests it, but our house payment makes me check any risk twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team that a little helper can draft test cases for overdue notices, but a person should check the amount before it goes to a library member. We would still have the same releases and desk calls. I wouldn't make a fuss about a small time saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and my partner's bus-repair wage would hold up. Four months saved helps with a broken boiler or a slow month. The mortgage is there, but we're paying it on schedule and I don't expect a cut from this modest change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing notices with a senior review and use the helper only on old test cases after the team approves it. We'd continue the automatic savings transfer we already make each payday. In the first year I'd keep a record of any wrong fine the helper misses before letting it near live notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The house payment takes planning, but it isn't keeping me awake today. A tool that saves a little time and leaves the work in our hands feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wrong fine would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A child returned a book on time but the system sent a late notice after a holiday. I'd use that old case to see whether the helper notices the date. I wouldn't let a software test send a library fine on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your savings target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have four months put by and a regular transfer that still leaves money for food. I'd rather keep that steady than chase a new target because of a tool. My partner and I review it twice a year.

say: I'd use a **small helper** for old notice tests while people check every amount.
I'd expect the **release schedule** and library calls to stay familiar.
think: I expect both **household wages** to continue under modest AI change.
Our **four-month savings** absorb ordinary surprises while the mortgage stays on schedule.
do: Keep **fixing library notices** with senior review before releases.
Continue our **payday savings transfer** and log wrong fines before using AI on live notices.
feel: **Calm** about current pay and the mortgage, with a manageable small tool.
S0.quote: I wouldn't let a software test send a library fine on its own.
fieldNote: Her caution is tied to a **wrong fine** sent to a child, not opposition to every tool.
Typical pay, a bus-repair wage and **four months saved** support calm today.
She keeps an **existing savings habit** because it already fits the household budget.

steps.text: Keep fixing library overdue notices with senior code review
Continue an affordable savings transfer from each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say routine coding and patron replies might go to AI, so we should tell staff how many junior hours are at risk. I'd ask the libraries to test the new notices with real return records. We shouldn't make library members pay for a faster software mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The easy fixes I do could be the first ones handed to a machine. I might keep a few hours checking errors, but our mortgage needs a proper wage. My partner's repair pay helps, yet it wouldn't replace my whole income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd ask for a three-week trial on past overdue errors, with a senior developer checking the results. I'd learn the new notice tool on paid time if management permits and keep examples of where it fails. If my hours fall in the first year, we'd cancel the planned spring trip and I'd apply to nearby library-software support roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn the tool if somebody proves it works, and we have four months saved. I still feel a knot when I picture the junior rota with fewer names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a library member with a wrong notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the member a person will check the return record and correct the fine. I'd want the library to have that phone number on the notice. A faster answer is no comfort if it sends them around in circles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the tool to catch the holiday return and three other known mistakes before live use. If it misses one, a senior colleague and I should inspect the rule. I won't call it ready just because it writes clean text.

say: I'd ask for **junior-hour numbers** as AI takes routine code and patron replies.
I'd demand **real return tests** before libraries send automated notices.
think: I could lose **paid junior hours** because routine fixes are much of my work.
My partner's **repair wage** cannot replace my whole income or carry the mortgage alone.
do: Run a **three-week trial** on old overdue errors with senior review next month.
Learn the **new notice tool** on paid time if management allows it.
Cancel the **spring trip** and apply for local library-software support if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced junior hours, with some savings and a tested learning route.
S1.quote: We shouldn't make library members pay for a faster software mistake.
fieldNote: She names **specific old errors** as a gate before live AI notices.
Her junior workload overlaps **routine writing and checking**, making fewer paid hours plausible.
The holiday cancellation and local search remain **conditional on reduced hours**.

steps.text: Learn the new notice tool on paid time during a reviewed trial if permitted
Cancel the planned spring trip if paid developer hours fall
Apply for nearby library software support vacancies if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team full thinking AI by 2028 could write our code and check notices before robots reach bus repair around 2031. I'd ask for a written staffing date and a human route for disputing fines. My partner's hands-on job has a later clock, but I wouldn't call it permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer role could go. Four months saved would give us some time, but the mortgage and two children would use it quickly. My partner's repair wage might continue until physical robots arrive, and then we could face another change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the library support manager about paid desk vacancies and request a reference from my developer manager. We'd cancel a planned appliance upgrade and put new spare pay into the emergency account while both wages last. In the first year after 2028, if I lose the developer job, I'd apply for a paid library desk role if one exists and contact the lender before a missed mortgage payment; I would take a library administration course only if a vacancy requires it and the fee leaves four months of essentials intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make calls, but I expect a big piece of our income to disappear before I've learned another paid role. Four months of savings is not a long bridge for a family of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the appliance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children we can keep using the old fridge unless it stops working. I wouldn't make a big speech about AI at dinner. They would notice a missed house payment long before a delayed fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the library desk job be automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, parts of it could. I'd ask the manager which tasks still need a person and what the hours pay, not assume it is a safe forever job. I would not pay for a course without a real opening.

say: I'd seek a **written staffing date** as 2028 thinking AI reaches library code.
I'd insist on a **human fine appeal** and separate later bus-repair robots from my screen job.
think: I expect my **junior wage** could disappear and four months saved could run out quickly.
My partner's **bus-repair wage** may last longer, yet later robots could affect that work too.
do: Ask about **paid library desk vacancies** now and request a developer reference.
Cancel the **appliance upgrade** and save new spare pay while both wages last.
Apply for **paid desk work** after layoff and call the lender before missed payment; study only with required vacancies and protected savings.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and only a four-month bridge for the household.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is not a long bridge for a family of four.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 thinking AI** from robots affecting bus repair around 2031.
The appliance cancellation is a **spending cut**; spare new pay goes into savings while both wages last.
Desk work and a course require **actual vacancies**, a fee she can pay and protected essentials.

steps.text: Cancel the planned appliance upgrade before 2028
Transfer new spare pay into emergency savings while both wages continue
Apply for paid library desk vacancies if the developer job ends
Take library administration course only if paid vacancy requires it and four months of essentials remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to publish a yearly count of junior jobs and let us see how libraries handle complaints. Five years could be used well, but thinking AI in 2031 still reaches our code before robots reach bus repair around 2034. I'd rather have a training timetable than a reassuring slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the library's customer side and build a larger buffer by 2031. I don't know whether libraries will still hire desk staff once AI handles many replies. Our mortgage means any move has to be paid, not an unpaid chance to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd enroll in a short library administration course if the employer pays the fee and gives me work time; otherwise I'd only pay from new savings above four months of essentials if paid vacancies require the course. We'd transfer a fixed affordable amount from each pay cheque toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2031, if my coding hours fall and a paid library role is open, I'd apply before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years gives me a chance to learn without throwing away the wage we have. It still doesn't promise the library desk will need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach that coding hasn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how a library checks a disputed fine and speaks to a member whose borrowing record is wrong. Code review only shows me the screen side of a disputed library fine. I want to hear what a useful correction sounds like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the monthly transfer is too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lower it before missing the mortgage, then restart when the next pay cheque allows it. We can aim for six months without pretending every month is the same. My partner and I would review the balance twice a year.

say: I'd demand a **yearly junior count** and a real training timetable before 2031.
I'd note that **2034 robots** may affect bus repair after our screen work changes.
think: I could gain **library administration skills** and savings over five years.
I need a **paid role**, since the mortgage cannot wait for an unpaid career trial.
do: Enroll in a **library course** only with employer-paid time and fee, or required vacancies and new savings beyond four months.
Transfer an **affordable pay share** toward six months of expenses, lowering it before missing the mortgage.
Apply for **paid library roles** if coding hours fall after 2031 and vacancies exist.
feel: **Anxious** about future income, with time to learn while keeping the current wage.
S3.quote: Code review only shows me the screen side of a disputed library fine.
fieldNote: She wants to learn the **member complaint**, not simply another screen task.
Training requires **paid time** or **protected savings**, with any self-funded course tied to real vacancies.
She sets a **six-month savings target** but lowers transfers before risking the mortgage.

steps.text: Enroll in employer-funded paid-time library course or self-fund only for required vacancies beyond four months
Transfer affordable pay amounts toward six months of expenses without missing mortgage
Apply for paid library vacancies if coding hours fall after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children ten years is enough time to learn something new, but people still have to check whether a notice is fair. I'd ask the company to train junior staff with libraries while there is time. Thinking AI in 2036 changes code before bus-repair robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might move past junior work or have paid library experience by my early fifties. Four months saved and two wages make today stable, but a mortgage lasts longer than ten years. I would want actual pay in any new role, not a promise that people will always be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer job and our regular savings transfer, then ask for a paid library placement one day a month if my employer agrees. I'd complete a library administration course only if the employer funds it or new savings above four months cover the fee after the mortgage. In the first year after 2036, if developer hours shrink and a paid library opening exists, I'd apply while keeping any paid development hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's enough time to make a careful move, and the bills are covered now. I would miss writing code if the job changed, but I wouldn't feel trapped today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the placement useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with a librarian correcting a child’s wrong fine and follow the case until the family hears back. One afternoon of watching software isn't enough. I want to know whether I can do the person-facing part well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the company never offers a placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask nearby libraries about paid openings and requirements before buying any course. I wouldn't use the mortgage reserve to purchase a hopeful certificate. We can keep saving while I have developer work.

say: I'd ask for **paid library placements** while the decade allows training.
I'd remind colleagues that **2036 thinking AI** reaches code before later bus-repair robots.
think: I could have **paid library experience** or stronger development skills by my early fifties.
I would judge any move by **actual wages**, with a long mortgage still ahead.
do: Keep **developer work** and regular savings transfers while paid hours remain.
Complete a **library course** only if employer-funded or payable from new savings beyond four months after mortgage.
Apply for **paid library vacancies** if developer hours shrink after 2036, keeping any paid coding work meanwhile.
feel: **Uneasy** about a later career change, with current wages and savings keeping the household stable.
S4.quote: I wouldn't use the mortgage reserve to purchase a hopeful certificate.
fieldNote: The decade lets her test **person-facing library work** while maintaining a developer wage.
A course is **conditional on funding** beyond the household's four-month reserve.
She would keep any **paid coding hours** until a real library opening exists.

steps.text: Keep paid developer work while coding hours remain
Continue affordable payday transfers into household savings
Complete library course only if employer-funded or paid beyond four-month reserve after mortgage
Apply for paid library vacancies if coding hours shrink after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My junior code and notice checking could end before I have a paid library alternative, and four months of expenses would not carry the mortgage for long. Written notice, employer-paid library training and real paid openings would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a family does with an unfair fine while the software argues back. A child can be shut out of library borrowing over a small software mistake. I want a person at the library who can fix the record before the family gives up.

headlineQuote: A child can be shut out of library borrowing over a small software mistake.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, fixing library lending software while still learning.
She has **typical pay**, a bus-repair partner, two school-age children, a mortgage and four months saved.
She uses AI **occasionally** after colleagues test it, and checks notices against real borrowing records.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because her junior wage could go before a paid library alternative appears.
Longer timelines let her seek **library administration training**, with mortgage, funding and vacancy conditions explicit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior wage before she secures paid library work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, employer-paid library training and real paid openings would help her protect the mortgage.
